newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Maskhadov seen as favourite in Chechen poll.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Maskhadov seen as favourite in Chechen poll.

text.p: Chieftains of Chechnya's guerrilla struggle against Russia are exchanging battle dress for suits as they prepare for elections for the post-war leadership of the rebel Moslem province.

After humiliating the Russian army in a series of defeats during which it failed to crush the tiny republic's independence drive, rebel leaders are embarking on political careers to try to capture the presidency and parliament on January 27.
Russian troops will complete their withdrawal from Chechnya before the elections, Russian news agencies quoted officials as saying on Monday.
Political observers say the failure to field a single presidential candidate for the post is a friendly "split" which does not mean the end of their wartime solidarity.
Of 19 candidates who initially hoped to contest the presidency only four have managed to gather the 10,000 signatures in petitions of support required to enter the race.
They include the main separatist field commanders and political figures.
Only Dzhokhar Dudayev, the charismatic godfather of the Chechen independence movement who was presumed killed in a Russian rocket attack last spring, is missing from the list.
MASKHADOV FAVOURITE TO SUCCEED

Among his would-be successors are Shamil Basayev, hailed as a hero at home but reviled in Russia as a terrorist, the wily information minister Movladi Udugov and Chechnya's acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, a bearded poet and lover of exotic birds.

But observers say the clear favourite is Aslan Maskhadov, Dudayev's soft-spoken chief commander who not only led the rebels to stunning battlefield successes but took up the reins in peace negotiations that led to the Russian pullout.

"Maskhadov is extremely popular right now. I can't imagine anyone posing a truly serious threat to him for the presidency," said Professor Aslan Dakayev of the Chechen State University in the regional capital Grozny.
Maskhadov, who coordinated the guerrilla army that harried the Russians with relentless sneak attacks, has proved himself a master military tactician.
The negotiations showed he has more than an aptitude for making war, and that seems to be the defining factor in his popularity.
MASKHADOV'S RESTRAINT MASKS STRONG SEPARATIST VIEWS

"Maskhadov is very rational and calm, and he gives people hope that the next five years can bring at least some stability in their lives. Everyone is sick of war and upheavals," said Dakayev, whose university was devastated by bombing during the war.
His students now take classes in an unheated, partially unfinished cement apartment building.
While Maskhadov, a 45-year-old former colonel shares a Red Army past with Dudayev and remained loyal to him to the end, their personalities and leadership styles contrast starkly.

The volatile, moustachioed Dudayev, was known for his rambling tirades which led some Russian politicians to dismiss him as mad. A dramatic orator, he was often a rather foppish dresser who reviewed parades through Grozny wearing black Fedora hats and white gloves.
The grey-haired Maskhadov, with his gentle smile and almost meek manner, is the picture of restraint.

Despite having led the stubborn rebel resistance, he was immediately identified by the Russian leadership as someone it could work with and it was Maskhadov with whom it eventually signed a peace agreement ending the war.
In the end Moscow gave in to almost every Chechen demand in exchange only for a vague promise to put off deciding the region's status for five years.

"He (Dudayev) was rigid and loved emotion, while I always said we shouldn't rush to war. But on the question of Chechen independence, I don't differ one iota from him. We are an independent country," Maskhadov told Reuters recently.
MASKHADOV'S PRAGMATISM LIKELY TO WIN VOTES
Potential voters who say they have made up their minds to vote for Maskhadov say his pragmatism is as important to them as his status as a national war hero.

"Right now we need someone with a cool head, someone whom the outside world will respect as our leader," said Alvi, a former fighter who now is part of the separatist government's police force in Grozny.

Alvi and many other Chechens say they admire Shamil Basayev, the gutsy field commander who forced Russia to the negotiating table with a bloody hostage-taking mission in 1995, but the election of such a figure would risk putting Chechnya on a new collision course with Moscow.
"If Basayev were president we'd have five years of more problems with Russia," Alvi said.

Dakayev agreed: "It's not that people think that Russia is going to come in and rebuild the republic, but at least there might be some normality to life and fewer conflicts with Moscow if Maskhadov is running things."
Dakayev put Basayev's chances of winning the election at "absolutely zero".
NO SPLINTERING SEEN IN REBEL RANKS
The prospect of the stern-faced, bearded Basayev, widely feared in Russia, posing with Russian leaders for photo opportunities must send shivers down the spine of the Kremlin.
Yandarbiyev is also given little chance of winning.
Dudayev's low-key ideology chief and vice-president, he took power automatically when the leader was killed last year but has never enjoyed strong personal popularity.
"Yandarbiyev does not inspire people as a national hero and he was not one of the military leaders of the resistance," said Dakayev.

Maskhadov has called the failure to field a single separatist candidate "unfortunate" but he and his aides say it does not mean the movement will splinter into warring factions as happened in Afghanistan.
There is little sign of hostility among the candidates, who continue to work in a coalition government until the elections.
"There is no animosity. They are all still friends but each has decided that they must do what they must do," said one of Maskhadov's senior political aides.
